Bonded Strain Gauge Diagram: Parts and Layout

Bonded strain gauge diagram drawings show a thin metal foil or wire grid glued onto the surface that is being strained, usually a flexible diaphragm in a pressure sensor. When the diaphragm bends, the grid stretches or compresses with it and its resistance changes. The table lists each part you will see in a typical diagram and what it does.

Part in the diagramWhat it isFunction
Diaphragm or test surfaceFlexible metal elementBends under pressure or force and carries the strain
Adhesive layerThin bonding cementTransfers the strain from the surface to the gauge
Backing or carrierThin insulating filmHolds the grid and insulates it from the metal surface
Sensing gridZigzag foil or fine wireChanges resistance as it gets longer and thinner or shorter and thicker
Solder tabs and lead wiresWide end pads and leadsConnect the grid to the Wheatstone bridge

How the Four Gauges Are Arranged

  1. Two gauges are bonded near the centre of the diaphragm to sense tangential strain.
  2. Two gauges are bonded near the edge to sense radial strain, which has the opposite sign.
  3. The four gauges are wired as the four arms of a Wheatstone bridge.
  4. As pressure rises, two arms increase in resistance and two decrease, so the bridge output adds up and temperature effects largely cancel.

The sensitivity of the grid is given by the gauge factor, GF = (ΔR ÷ R) ÷ strain. Metal foil gauges have a gauge factor of about 2, so a strain of 1000 microstrain gives a resistance change of about 0.2 percent, which is why a bridge circuit is needed to read it.
